This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/features/calendar-cache/calendar-cache.repository.ts:176 — Cache status includes expired rows that runtime cache reads reject, so the UI can silently claim a usable cache exists when every availability lookup is a cache miss.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real issue. Looking at the diff, `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` in calendar-cache.repository.ts (lines 172-189) queries CalendarCache and returns the max `updatedAt` without filtering by `expiresAt`. The existing `watchCalendar` method at line 169 shows cache entries have an `expiresAt` field used for expiration. The UI displays cache status based on `updatedAt` (shown in CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx lines 85-93), but if all cache entries are expired (expiresAt < now), the runtime cache reads would reject them while the UI still shows a valid cache timestamp. This is a correctness bug where the UI can mislead users about cache availability.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/features/calendar-cache/calendar-cache.repository.ts:179 — Taking the maximum timestamp across per-key cache rows makes a partially failed sequential refresh look fully current, masking stale availability for calendar groups whose refresh failed.

adjudication.rationale: The finding points to a real architectural concern in the new getCacheStatusByCredentialIds method at line 172-189. The method uses groupBy with _max on updatedAt to get the most recent cache timestamp per credential. If a credential has multiple calendar cache entries and only some were successfully refreshed, the max timestamp would show the latest successful one, potentially masking that other calendars under the same credential have stale data. However, this is a design/architecture concern rather than a bug - the feature is working as implemented, but the implementation choice of showing only the max timestamp could be misleading. This is a legitimate scope concern about the new functionality being added.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/features/apps/components/CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx:43 — A successful cache deletion never invalidates connectedCalendars, so callers without a refetching onSuccess callback keep showing the deleted cache and allow repeated misleading deletes.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the deleteCacheMutation in CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx (lines 43-51), the onSuccess callback only shows a toast and calls onSuccess?.(). Unlike the disconnectMutation (lines 53-66) which has an onSettled that invalidates connectedCalendars and integrations queries, the deleteCacheMutation has no query invalidation. This means after deleting the cache, the UI won't refresh to reflect the deleted cache status (cacheUpdatedAt would still show the old value). The connectedCalendars query that provides cacheUpdatedAt (as shown in connectedCalendars.handler.ts) is never invalidated after cache deletion, so the dropdown will continue showing stale cache status information.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/calendars/_router.tsx:29 — The credentialId schema accepts fractional and non-finite numbers instead of an integer database identifier, so malformed requests cross the API boundary and produce misleading lookup or internal errors rather than validation failures.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims z.number() accepts fractional and non-finite numbers, which is technically true for z.number() alone. However, this is a very minor validation concern - Prisma will handle the integer conversion at the database layer, and the actual behavior would be that fractional numbers get truncated or cause a database error, not 'misleading lookup errors'. The finding overstates the severity. More importantly, using z.number() for IDs is a common pattern in the codebase (as seen in other parts of the diff like DisconnectIntegration), and this is more of a style/best-practice suggestion than a real defect. The code will work correctly for valid integer inputs, which is the expected use case.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:1024 — Passing an empty update payload does not advance Prisma's `@updatedAt` field, so successful cache rebuilds never record the intended refresh time on selected calendars.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {});` being called with an empty object `{}` as the data parameter. Looking at the repository method in the diff: `static async updateManyByCredentialId(credentialId: number, data: Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput) { return await prisma.selectedCalendar.updateMany({ where: { credentialId }, data }); }`. Prisma's `@updatedAt` decorator only auto-updates when there's an actual field change in the update operation. Passing an empty `data: {}` object means no fields are being updated, so Prisma won't trigger the `@updatedAt` auto-update. The intent appears to be to update the `updatedAt` timestamp to track cache refresh times (as evidenced by the comment 'Update SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for all calendars under this credential'), but this implementation won't achieve that goal.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/features/apps/components/CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx:42 — The cache-delete mutation never invalidates `connectedCalendars` and its optional callback may be absent, so the UI can keep reporting a deleted cache as present after success.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, the deleteCacheMutation in CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx (lines 42-50) only calls onSuccess?.() callback but does NOT invalidate connectedCalendars. In contrast, the disconnectMutation (lines 52-66) has an onSettled handler that explicitly invalidates both connectedCalendars and integrations. The connectedCalendars handler (connectedCalendars.handler.ts) fetches cacheUpdatedAt from the cache repository and returns it with the calendar data. After deleting the cache, without invalidating connectedCalendars, the UI will continue showing the stale cacheUpdatedAt value until a manual refresh. The onSuccess callback is optional and may not trigger a refetch. This is a real bug where the cache status UI won't update after deletion.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/prisma/migrations/20250715160635_add_calendar_cache_updated_at/migration.sql:9 — This alters a previously committed empty migration, so databases that already recorded it as applied will never add `CalendarCache.updatedAt` and the newly deployed queries will fail at runtime.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims this migration 'alters a previously committed empty migration' but there's no evidence in the diff that this migration was previously committed as empty. The diff shows a new migration file being added (20250715160635_add_calendar_cache_updated_at/migration.sql) with the full content including the ALTER TABLE statement. This appears to be a new migration being introduced in this PR, not a modification of an existing empty migration. The migration file path shows it's being created (diff shows 'new file mode') and contains the complete ALTER TABLE statement to add the updatedAt column.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/calendars/connectedCalendars.handler.ts:28 — Constructing the concrete CalendarCacheRepository in the handler bypasses the cache-disabled/mock boundary, coupling this UI query to the production persistence implementation and forcing future backends to change the handler.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the handler directly instantiates CalendarCacheRepository instead of using dependency injection or the mock pattern. Looking at the diff, there's a CalendarCacheRepositoryMock class (calendar-cache.repository.mock.ts) that implements the same interface with stub methods for when calendar-cache is disabled. The handler at line 28 does `new CalendarCacheRepository()` directly, bypassing this mock boundary. This is a legitimate architectural concern - the code creates tight coupling to the concrete implementation rather than using the abstraction pattern established elsewhere in the codebase. However, this is a design/architecture issue, not a bug that would cause incorrect behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/calendars/deleteCache.handler.ts:28 — Deleting CalendarCache rows through Prisma creates a second persistence path outside the calendar-cache repository, so cache backend and disabled-mode changes must be duplicated here.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies an architectural concern. The diff shows that CalendarCacheRepository exists (calendar-cache.repository.ts) with methods like deleteManyByCredential(), and there's also a mock implementation (calendar-cache.repository.mock.ts) that handles disabled-mode by logging and skipping operations. However, the new deleteCache.handler.ts directly uses prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany() instead of going through the repository. This bypasses the repository pattern and the disabled-mode handling in the mock. This is a legitimate architectural concern about consistency - if calendar-cache is disabled, the mock's behavior won't apply to this new handler.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:1024 — Updating every SelectedCalendar timestamp after filling CalendarCache is dead cross-model bookkeeping because the new status flow reads CalendarCache.updatedAt, adding writes and a one-off repository method with misleading semantics.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims the SelectedCalendar.updatedAt update is 'dead cross-model bookkeeping' because the status flow reads CalendarCache.updatedAt. However, examining the diff shows that the cacheUpdatedAt displayed in the UI comes from CalendarCacheRepository.getCacheStatusByCredentialIds() which reads CalendarCache.updatedAt (via groupBy with _max.updatedAt), NOT from SelectedCalendar.updatedAt. The SelectedCalendar.updateManyByCredentialId call with empty data {} will trigger the @updatedAt decorator on SelectedCalendar records, but this is separate from the cache status display. While this may be unnecessary bookkeeping, it's not 'dead' - it could serve other purposes not visible in this diff. The finding mischaracterizes the relationship between these updates.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/lib/getConnectedDestinationCalendars.ts:23 — Requiring updatedAt and googleChannelId on UserWithCalendars leaks unused SelectedCalendar fields through the session/query boundary, forcing unrelated callers and database selects to carry data this flow never reads.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims these fields are 'unused' and 'leak' through boundaries, but examining the diff shows: 1) updatedAt is used - it's selected in user.ts repository and flows through to cacheUpdatedAt in the connected calendars response, which is then used by CredentialActionsDropdown to display cache status. 2) googleChannelId is added to the type but the diff shows it being selected in the repository query. The fields are not 'unused' - they serve the new cache status feature being implemented. The finding misreads the purpose of these additions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/features/calendar-cache/calendar-cache.repository.ts:176 — The status aggregation includes expired rows that are never purged, so every connected-calendars request scans an ever-growing per-credential cache history and will degrade as stale keys accumulate.

adjudication.rationale: The finding points to a real concern in the new getCacheStatusByCredentialIds method at line 172-189. The method queries CalendarCache grouped by credentialId without filtering by expiresAt, meaning it includes expired cache entries in the aggregation. While CalendarCache has an expiresAt field (visible in schema.prisma), the new query doesn't filter out expired rows. However, this is not strictly a 'bug' since the method returns the most recent updatedAt timestamp which could still be valid information. The concern about performance degradation is architectural - if expired rows are never purged, the table grows indefinitely. This is a legitimate scope/architecture concern introduced by the change, but not a correctness defect since the query still returns valid data about when cache was last updated.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/calendars/connectedCalendars.handler.ts:29 — An unhandled failure in the optional cache-status query now rejects the entire connected-calendars request, making calendar settings unavailable instead of degrading to a missing status.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff in connectedCalendars.handler.ts, the code adds `await cacheRepository.getCacheStatusByCredentialIds(credentialIds)` at line 29. This is a direct await without any try-catch wrapper. If this database query fails (network issue, database error, etc.), the entire handler will throw an exception and reject the request. Previously, the connected calendars endpoint would work without this cache status query. Now, a failure in this optional/supplementary cache status lookup will cause the entire calendar settings page to fail. This is a real bug - the cache status is enhancement information that should degrade gracefully rather than breaking the core functionality.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/features/apps/components/CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx:45 — The mutation success handler discards the Promise-capable onSuccess callback, so a failed async refresh becomes an unhandled rejection while the UI has already reported success and can remain stale.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at line 45 in CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx, the onSuccess callback is called with `onSuccess?.()` which is a standard optional chaining call. The finding claims this 'discards the Promise-capable onSuccess callback' leading to unhandled rejections, but this is incorrect. The optional chaining `?.()` properly invokes the callback if it exists. If onSuccess returns a Promise, not awaiting it doesn't cause an 'unhandled rejection' - it simply means the code doesn't wait for it. The callback is passed as `onSuccess?: () => void` in the interface, indicating it's not expected to be async. This is a standard pattern and not a bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh:17 — cleanup always exits with status 0 even when tunnel initialization or URL extraction fails, so callers cannot detect setup failure and may continue with a stale webhook URL.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the cleanup function in the diff (lines 14-21), it always calls 'exit 0' regardless of how it was invoked. The script calls cleanup() explicitly when rate limit is hit (line 47) and when URL extraction fails (line 60), but in both cases the exit code will be 0 (success) instead of a non-zero error code. This means any calling script or CI system cannot detect that the tunnel setup failed, which is a real defect in the script's error handling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:1024 — No database-backed test covers the new timestamp touch, and Prisma treats the empty update payload as a no-op, so cache rebuilds do not advance the intended selected-calendar status.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {});` being called with an empty object `{}` as the data parameter. Looking at the repository method in the diff: `static async updateManyByCredentialId(credentialId: number, data: Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput) { return await prisma.selectedCalendar.updateMany({ where: { credentialId }, data }); }` - passing an empty object means no fields are actually updated. While Prisma's `updateMany` with empty data might still trigger `@updatedAt` fields if they exist on the model, the comment says 'Update SelectedCalendar.updatedAt' but the code passes no actual data to update. The SelectedCalendar model does have an updatedAt field (as shown in the diff where it's selected), but Prisma's updateMany with empty data object is indeed a no-op that won't trigger @updatedAt. This is a real bug where the intended timestamp update won't occur.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/features/calendar-cache/calendar-cache.repository.ts:176 — No expired-row case is covered and the status query omits an expiresAt predicate, so unusable stale entries are presented as an active cache.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that getCacheStatusByCredentialIds in calendar-cache.repository.ts (lines 172-189) queries CalendarCache entries without filtering by expiresAt. The method returns the max updatedAt for each credentialId, but doesn't exclude expired cache entries. This means the UI could show 'cache last updated' timestamps for entries that have already expired and are no longer valid/usable. Looking at the diff, the query uses groupBy with _max on updatedAt but has no 'expiresAt: { gt: new Date() }' predicate in the where clause. This is a real correctness issue where stale/expired cache entries would be presented as active cache status.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/features/apps/components/CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx:42 — No post-delete UI test covers the optional-callback path, and the mutation does not invalidate connectedCalendars, so a successful deletion can leave the cache status and action visible until reload.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that deleteCacheMutation (lines 42-51) does not call utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate() after success, unlike disconnectMutation (lines 53-66) which does invalidate both connectedCalendars and apps.integrations. This means after deleting the cache, the UI will still show the old cacheUpdatedAt value until a manual refresh, since the connectedCalendars query that provides cacheUpdatedAt won't be refetched. This is a real behavioral bug where the UI becomes stale after a successful cache deletion.
